notes.meaning: Solomon made a peace treaty with Egypt by marrying the Pharaoh's daughter. Royal marriages like this were common in the ancient world to protect borders and open trade routes. He brought her to live in the City of David while his palace, the temple, and Jerusalem's outer walls were still being built.

The people of Israel were still offering sacrifices on local hilltop altars called high places. They did this because a single central temple dedicated to the Lord had not yet been built. While altars on hills were later banned to prevent idol worship, the people used them at this time as temporary places of worship.

Solomon loved the Lord and followed the godly teaching and commands given by his father David. His worship was genuine, but he still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. The writer notes this habit as an imperfection in an otherwise faithful start to his reign.

Solomon went to the town of Gibeon to worship because the sacred tent and the bronze altar from Moses' time were kept there. It was known as the chief place of worship before the temple was built. The king showed deep loyalty and generous devotion to God by offering one thousand burnt offerings on the altar.

The Lord appeared to Solomon during the night at Gibeon through a special dream. God gave the young king an open invitation to ask for whatever gift he desired. This was an invitation from the Lord to see what mattered most in Solomon's heart.

Solomon began his prayer by praising God for His faithful love to his father David. David had served God with an honest and upright heart, and God had kept His covenant promises to him. Solomon recognized that his own place on the throne was a direct result of God's steady mercy.

Solomon humbly called himself a little child before the Lord. He was a grown young man in years, but he felt completely inexperienced in running a kingdom. He knew he lacked the skill and training needed to lead the nation well on his own.

Solomon remembered that he was ruling God's chosen people, not a kingdom of his own making. The nation had grown so large that its people were too numerous to count. This massive population was a reminder of God's ancient promise to multiply Abraham's descendants.

Solomon asked the Lord for a listening and understanding heart to govern the people well. He wanted the ability to tell right from wrong so he could decide legal disputes fairly. He realized that no human leader could rule God's people without wisdom from above.

The Lord was very pleased with Solomon's request. Instead of asking for selfish advantages, the king had focused on what would best serve the nation. God welcomed a prayer that put the good of others ahead of personal desire.

God noted the things Solomon chose not to request, such as a long life, great wealth, or victory over military enemies. Most earthly kings wanted power, riches, and revenge more than anything else. Solomon had instead asked for the skill to govern with justice.

God granted Solomon's petition right away by giving him an exceptionally wise and discerning mind. His understanding would be so deep that no king before him or after him would match his insight. This gift set him apart as a uniquely gifted ruler.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this divine promise as a royal legend meant to explain Solomon's later fame as a wise ruler, noting that later books like Chronicles retell his story while glossing over his flaws.

notes.meaning: God also promised to give Solomon the blessings he had not asked for, including great riches and royal honor. Because he sought God's righteousness first, these extra gifts were freely added to his life. No other king in his lifetime would match his wealth and renown.

God added a conditional promise of a long life. If Solomon continued to obey God's laws and walk faithfully as David had done, God would lengthen his days. Unlike the promise of wisdom and riches, this blessing required lifelong obedience.

When Solomon woke up, he knew that the dream was a real message from God. He went straight to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant, which held God's law. There he presented thank-offerings to the Lord and held a celebratory meal for his royal officials.

Two women who were prostitutes brought a difficult legal problem directly to the king. In ancient Israel, such women held very low social standing and had little help in court. Solomon showed that his royal justice was open even to the humblest and most despised citizens.
The first woman spoke first and explained that both of them lived together in the same house. She told the king that she had given birth to a baby boy while the other woman was present.

Just three days after the first baby was born, the other woman gave birth to a son as well. No other people lived in the house, and no visitors were there to see what happened. This meant there were no witnesses who could settle any dispute between them.
During the night, the second woman's child died when she accidentally rolled over him in her sleep. The infant suffocated, leaving one living child and one dead child in the house.

The first woman claimed that the other mother woke up at midnight and traded the babies. While the first mother was asleep, the other woman took the living child and left the dead baby in her arms. She did this to cover up her mistake and keep a living son.

When the mother woke up in the morning to nurse her baby, she discovered the infant in her arms was dead. Once the morning light filled the room, she looked closely at the baby's features and realized it was not the child she had borne.

The second woman strongly denied the accusation, claiming that the living child was hers and the dead child belonged to the first woman. The first mother insisted just as loudly that the living baby was hers. They argued back and forth in front of Solomon, with only their opposing claims as evidence.

Solomon restated each woman's argument to make the problem plain to everyone in the room. One woman claimed the living baby, and the other woman claimed the exact same thing. Without witnesses or evidence, mere words could not reveal who was telling the truth.
Solomon ordered an attendant to bring him a sword. The royal court was likely startled by this strange command, but they promptly brought the weapon to the king.

The king commanded that the living child be cut in two so each woman could have half. Solomon had no plan to harm the infant; he used this startling command to test the hearts of both women. He knew that the true mother's love would quickly reveal itself.

The real mother was overcome with love and pity for her child and begged the king to give the baby to the other woman alive. In contrast, the false claimant showed cold jealousy, telling the king to cut the child in two so neither woman would have him. The test revealed the true feelings of both women.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers, such as Jerome, interpreted this courtroom scene allegorically as a picture of the true Church showing compassion while the false synagogue was willing to see the child perish.

notes.meaning: Solomon delivered his final judgment, ordering the living child to be given to the woman who begged for his life. Her willingness to give up her child rather than see him die proved that she was the true mother.

The report of Solomon's wise ruling quickly traveled across all Israel. The people felt deep respect and awe for the king because they saw that God had placed divine wisdom in him to govern with justice.
